sections.heading: How to get a caption in seconds
sections.body:
Open the caption generator, add a photo or describe your post, and choose where it will go. A run takes a few seconds, and you do not need an account.

1. Open the [caption generator](https://caption-generator.lazur.app/).
2. Add a photo under Photo. It must be an image file up to 15 MB.
3. Or type a few words under Or describe it. You can use either input, or both.
4. Pick the platform: Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, Facebook or X.
5. Run it, then read all five options before you copy one.

Each option is ready to paste, and you can copy any of them with one click.

sections.heading: Photo, description or both
sections.body:
A photo gives the writer what is in the picture: the place, the people, the mood and any words you can read in the frame. A description gives it what the picture cannot show, such as why you took it, where it was taken or what happened just before the shot.

**Use both when the picture is only half the story.** A photo of a sunset with the words first trip to the coast in two years gives the captions a reason to exist. Keep the description short. A few words is enough, and you still get five options.

sections.heading: Five styles in every run
sections.body:
Each run gives five captions, and every one takes a different angle. You get a funny line, a short one, a thoughtful one, one that ends with a question, and a bold one. Pick the voice that fits the account, or take the best part of two and join them into one post.

Hashtags come with each caption where the platform uses them, 3 to 5 per caption. Delete any you do not want, and keep the ones that match what the post is about.

sections.heading: One platform at a time
sections.body:
The platform you pick changes how the captions are written. A caption for Instagram or TikTok can be short and visual. A LinkedIn caption can run longer and explain one point. Facebook and X each have their own feel, so choose the platform you will post to.

Run the tool again for each platform instead of copying one caption everywhere. A line that works on LinkedIn often reads wrong on TikTok, and the second run costs you only seconds.

sections.heading: Free runs and where it runs
sections.body:
You get 3 free runs a day. Leave an email and you get 3 more. There is no account and no app to install. The tool runs on Lazur's servers using Google Gemini, and it answers in about 1 to 3 seconds.

If you write posts by voice every day, Lazur does that in any app on your Mac. Hold two keys and talk, and it types into whatever app you are in.

The captions come back in a few seconds, and each one is ready to paste under your photo.

sections.heading: What the writer sees in your photo
sections.body:
The writer looks at the picture itself: the subject, the setting, the light and any words that show clearly in the frame. The captions come from that. It cannot know what happened outside the frame, so if the photo needs a backstory, add it in the description box.

Sharp photos give the writer more to work with. A blurry shot, or a screenshot with tiny text, gives vaguer captions, so use the clearest photo you have. Good light helps too, because the writer can make out the subject and the setting more clearly in a well-lit picture.

sections.heading: When the captions feel generic
sections.body:
If all five options sound alike or just list what is in the picture, add one detail that only you know. Type something like my first marathon, feet hurt, proud of it, instead of uploading the photo alone. Then run it again.

The second run uses the same photo plus your words, so the captions change to fit the story. Keep the description to a few lines. Long notes do not make the captions better, and a clear fact does.

sections.heading: Photos that work and files that do not
sections.body:
The tool takes image files up to 15 MB. A photo from a phone is usually well under that. If your file is larger, save a smaller copy and try again.

The tool is for still images. If you want a caption for a video clip, describe the clip in a few sentences instead, and the captions will follow that description. Pick a frame that shows the moment you want to talk about, because the writer works from what is in the picture.

sections.heading: Check the caption before you post
sections.body:
Read each caption before you post it. The writer can misread a detail, such as who is in the picture or where it was taken, so fix anything that is not true. Hashtags come with the options where the platform uses them. Remove any that do not fit the photo.

**The photo is the source, so check it against the photo.** If a caption names a place or a person, look at the picture again before you publish.

sections.heading: How to write an Instagram caption
sections.body:
You can make the caption in one run, then paste it into Instagram.

1. Open the [Instagram caption generator](https://caption-generator.lazur.app/instagram).
2. Add your photo, or describe the post in a few words, or do both.
3. Choose Instagram as the platform.
4. Run it and read all five options.
5. Copy the caption you like, open your post in Instagram, and paste it into the caption box before you share.

The options come with hashtags where Instagram uses them, so you do not need to look up tags first.

sections.heading: Pick the style for the post
sections.body:
A funny caption suits a photo with a joke in it. A short one works when the picture already carries the post. A thoughtful caption fits a personal moment. A caption that ends with a question gets people to reply in the comments, and a bold line works for a launch or a claim you stand behind.

Read all five before you choose. Pick the one that sounds like you on a good day, not the most polished one. A caption you can say out loud without wincing is usually the right one for your account.

sections.heading: Hook first, details second
sections.body:
The first line of your caption is what people read first in the feed, so it does most of the work. If an option starts slowly, move a stronger line from another option to the top and keep the rest. A hook can be a question, a surprise or one short statement, and any of them works when it is true to the post. Read the caption out loud once, and cut any words that do not add anything.

The details can follow in the second and third lines: the place, the event, the thing you want people to do. Keep the caption short enough that the point is clear in a glance.

sections.heading: Hashtags: 3 to 5 per caption
sections.body:
Each caption comes with 3 to 5 hashtags where Instagram uses them. Hashtags help people find posts about a topic, so choose the ones that match what is in your photo. Delete any that feel off.

Do not paste the same block of hashtags under every post without checking it. A tag that fits one photo may have nothing to do with the next, and a post with unrelated tags does not help anyone find it.

sections.heading: Check the details before you post
sections.body:
The caption is a draft. The writer can get a name, a place or a detail wrong, and it does not know your audience or your rules. Read it once more, change anything that is not true, and then post.

**Read it as a stranger would.** If a line only makes sense to you, rewrite it so someone who has never met you can follow it.

faq.a: A good Instagram caption opens with a line that makes someone stop, says one clear thing, and ends with a reason to react, such as a question or a call to comment. Use the generator to get five options in different styles, then pick the one that sounds like you.

faq.q: How do I caption a pic?
faq.a: Upload the picture to the caption generator, choose Instagram, and run it. Copy one of the five captions. Then open your post in Instagram and paste the caption into the caption box before you share.

faq.q: Is there a free Instagram caption generator?
faq.a: Yes. The Instagram caption generator on Lazur is free. You get 3 runs a day, and 3 more after you leave an email. No account is needed, and each run gives you five options.

sections.heading: What the tool reads from a Reel
sections.body:
The caption generator takes a photo or a written description. It does not take a video file, so it cannot watch your Reel. That is why the description matters. Tell it what happens in the clip, the opening second, the joke or the result, and why people should watch.

Use a photo when one frame sums up the Reel, such as the cover frame. Use a description when the clip moves: a sequence, a reveal or a step-by-step tutorial. If the Reel shows text on screen, such as a title card or a list, name it in the description. The captions can then echo the same words, so the post and the clip agree.

sections.heading: How to make a Reel caption
sections.body:
Work through these steps for each Reel you post.

1. Open the [Reel caption generator](https://caption-generator.lazur.app/best-instagram-reels).
2. Add a still frame from the Reel, or skip the photo.
3. Describe the Reel in a few sentences.
4. Choose Instagram as the platform.
5. Run it, copy the caption you like, and paste it into your Reel before you share.

Each run gives five options with hashtags, so you can pick a line that fits the clip and throw out the rest.

sections.heading: Describe the clip well
sections.body:
Compare two descriptions. Reel about my cat gives the writer almost nothing to work with. Cat knocks a mug off the desk, then looks at me like it did nothing. Funny, and I want people to tag a friend gives it the joke, the ending and the reason to share.

Name the action, the ending and the feeling you want. Keep it to a few sentences. The more specific the clip is in your words, the more the five options will sound like it.

sections.heading: Captions on the video itself
sections.body:
A caption on Instagram is the text you post under the Reel. If you want the spoken words shown on the video, that is a subtitle job, and this tool does not add text to a video. Use it for the post text, and use a subtitle tool for words that appear on screen.

Keeping the two apart saves time. The post caption tells people what the Reel is about, and the subtitles help people follow the words while they watch.

sections.heading: Check the caption against the clip
sections.body:
Read each option next to the clip. The writer does not see your video, so a detail like a place name or a claim about a product may be wrong. Fix it before you post. Keep the hashtags that match the clip and remove the rest.

**The description is the source, so check it against the Reel.** If a caption says something that did not happen on screen, change it before you share.

faq.q: How can I generate captions for Instagram Reels?
faq.a: Open the Reel caption generator, describe your Reel in a few sentences or add a still frame from it, choose Instagram, and run it. You get five caption options with hashtags. Copy one and paste it into your Reel before you share.

faq.q: What is the best caption for reels?
faq.a: There is no single best caption for every Reel. The right caption depends on what happens in the clip and who you want to reach. Describe your Reel to get five different styles, then pick the one that fits the clip and sounds like you.

faq.q: Can I caption a Reel from a video file?
faq.a: Not with this tool. The caption generator takes a photo or a written description, not a video file. Describe the clip in a few sentences, and the five captions will follow that description.
